TLS, the blocks together

Puzzles 0 to 7 each stopped one thing a machine in the middle could do. The S in HTTPS is those blocks put together in one short conversation before your first request.

Diagram Mechanism Check your understanding

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 6: A hash with a secret

    A MAC (message authentication code) is a short value computed from the data and a secret key together; HMAC builds one from a hash function. The sender attaches it as a tag; the receiver, who has the same key, recomputes it and compares. An attacker who changes the data can't compute the matching tag without the key, so any change is caught. TLS protects every chunk of your data this way.

  • Puzzle 7: Proof of who you are

    A key pair is a private key the owner keeps and a public key anyone may have. Signing computes a signature from a digest and the private key; anyone can check it with the public key, and nobody can fake it without the private key. A certificate is a server's name and public key, signed by a certificate authority your phone already trusts.

The problem

Puzzle 0 named three things a machine in the middle can do: read, change, pretend. Puzzles 1 to 7 each built one block: symmetric encryption, key exchange, hashes, signatures and certificates. Your app opens an https address and sends a request a moment later. How do all those blocks fit into that moment?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

TLS is the protocol behind HTTPS: a set of agreed messages and rules. Before any of your data is sent, the app and the server have a short exchange: the handshake. In TLS 1.3 (the current version) it takes one round trip, there and back:

  1. Your app says hello and sends its public value for a key exchange (puzzle 3).
  2. The server answers with its own public value. Now both sides compute the shared secret, and from it they derive several keys (computed from it by a fixed recipe both sides follow): one set for the rest of the handshake, another for your data. From this point on, everything is encrypted.
  3. Still in the handshake, but now encrypted, the server sends its certificate (puzzle 7) and a signature over the whole conversation so far, made with its private key.
  4. Your app checks the certificate against the authorities it trusts, checks the name against the address, and checks the signature. A listener with a copied certificate fails here: it can't make that signature.
  5. Both sides end the handshake with a MAC (puzzle 6) over everything said so far, called Finished. Only now does each know that nobody changed the handshake on the way.

Then your data flows in records: chunks of data, each sent and checked on its own. Each record goes through one combined step, called authenticated encryption, for example AES in a mode built for it: it encrypts the record and attaches a MAC (puzzle 6), called a tag, both computed with keys derived from the shared secret. A listener who changes a byte can't make a matching tag, because it doesn't have the keys, so the change is detected and the record rejected. Reading: stopped by encryption. Changing: stopped by the tag on every record. Pretending: stopped by the certificate and the signature.

TLS doesn't hide everything: someone in the middle still sees which server you talk to and how much data goes back and forth. It hides what is said, and makes sure it's said to the right server.

The analogy

A courier and a bank: first the bank shows its registered seal and you both agree on a code, in plain sight but in a way no one listening can copy. Then every envelope goes out in that code, sealed so any tampering shows.

Check yourself

Your app connects to your server over HTTPS on the café Wi-Fi. A machine in the middle replaces one byte of the response. What happens?

Right. Every record is checked as well as encrypted.

Not quite. Encryption alone wouldn't notice; the per-record check is what catches it.

Not quite. Every record carries a keyed check; a changed byte makes it fail, and the listener can't recompute it.

Why does the server sign the handshake, not only send its certificate?

Right. A certificate can be copied; a signature can't.

Not quite. The data is encrypted with symmetric keys from the key exchange, not with the signature.

Not quite. Size isn't the issue: a copied certificate proves nothing without a signature.

What's the difference between the handshake and everything after it?

Not quite. Afterwards everything is encrypted, with symmetric keys from the key exchange.

Right. Setting up vs using.

Sources
  • RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 (the handshake "can be thought of as having three phases": Key Exchange, "Everything after this phase is encrypted", then Server Parameters and Authentication with Certificate and CertificateVerify; "all ciphers are modeled as Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)… a unified encryption and authentication operation"; "TLS does not hide the length of the data it transmits")

What you now know

A TLS handshake does a key exchange, has the server prove who it is with its certificate and a signature, and turns the shared secret into symmetric keys. Everything after that is encrypted with an AES-style cipher that also detects changes. Reading, changing and pretending are all stopped.
